home.title: Solve your cube by following a path through a graph
home.intro: Every position of the cube is a vertex and every turn is an edge. Solving it means finding a path to the “solved” vertex. We guide you step by step: you make the turn, confirm it, and we show you what is happening in the graph.
home.hint: With the camera it reads one face at a time. If you would rather upload photos, two are enough: each one shows three faces, with a corner pointing at the camera.
home.e1.title: The sticker graph
home.e1.body: The 54 stickers are vertices. Each face turn moves them around a ring of 12 stickers and rotates the 8 of the face itself: those are the cycles of a permutation.
home.e2.title: The graph of states
home.e2.body: About 43 quintillion vertices, 18 edges per vertex and diameter 20 (“God's number”). Far too big to explore whole, so we split it into stages.
home.e3.title: Finding paths
home.e3.body: In each stage we use BFS to know the exact distance to the goal, or IDA* with lower bounds in the fast mode. Every step you confirm is an edge that brings you closer.

stage.cross.title: 1 · Bottom cross
stage.cross.goal: The four bottom edges in place and the right way round.
stage.cross.graph: Vertices: where the 4 bottom edges are and how they are turned. Edges of the graph: the 18 face turns.
stage.corners.title: 2 · Bottom corners
stage.corners.goal: The four bottom corners in place, completing the first layer.
stage.corners.graph: Vertices: position and twist of the 4 bottom corners. Edges: turn the top (U) or apply R U R' U' over one of the four slots (it does not break the cross).
stage.middle.title: 3 · Second layer
stage.middle.goal: The four middle-layer edges in place.
stage.middle.graph: Vertices: position and orientation of the 4 middle edges. Edges: turn the top or one of the 8 insertion algorithms (they do not break the first layer).
stage.eo.title: 4 · Top cross
stage.eo.goal: The four top edges with the top colour facing up.
stage.eo.graph: Vertices: position and orientation of the top edges. Edges: turn the top or F R U R' U' F'.
stage.co.title: 5 · Top face
stage.co.goal: The four top corners with the top colour facing up.
stage.co.graph: Vertices: position and twist of the top corners. Edges: turn the top, Sune or Antisune.
stage.cp.title: 6 · Top corners in place
stage.cp.goal: The top corners placed relative to each other (one turn of U lines them up).
stage.cp.graph: Vertices: position of the top corners. Edges: turn the top or an A-perm, which cycles three corners without twisting them.
stage.ep.title: 7 · Top edges in place
stage.ep.goal: All solved: top edges placed and the layer lined up.
stage.ep.graph: Vertices: position of the top corners and edges. Edges: turn the top or a U-perm, which cycles three edges without touching the corners.
stage.phase1.title: Phase 1 · Reach the subgroup H
stage.phase1.goal: Orient every piece and bring the 4 middle edges into their layer: from there on, U, D and half turns of the rest are enough.
stage.phase1.graph: Quotient graph G/H: 2,217,093,120 vertices (corner twist × edge orientation × position of the middle edges), 18 edges per vertex.
stage.phase2.title: Phase 2 · Solve inside H
stage.phase2.goal: Place every piece using only U, D, R2, L2, F2 and B2.
stage.phase2.graph: Subgraph H: 19,508,428,800 vertices, 10 edges per vertex (the moves that do not undo phase 1).

info.cube3d.title: The 3D cube
info.cube3d.html:
It is a twin of your cube. It always shows the state yours should be in just before the current step, and then animates the turn you have to make.

How to read it

  • The animation runs at the speed you set at the bottom right.
  • If the cube on the screen and yours stop matching, you have missed a turn: use “I'm lost” to scan again and work out the path again.

What you can do

  • Drag with the mouse or your finger to turn the view. This does not move the cube, only the camera: it is for looking round the back.
  • Scroll or pinch to zoom in and out.
  • ↻ replays the step's animation. ⌂ goes back to the initial view.

Tip: hold your cube the same way as the one on the screen, with the same colours on top and in front, and do not turn it whole during the solve.
info.step.title: The step card
info.step.html:
Each step is an edge of the graph: a single turn, or a whole algorithm when the stage works with algorithms. You make it on your cube and confirm it.

The notation

  • R, L, U, D, F, B: the right, left, up (top), down (bottom), front and back faces.
  • No symbol: a quarter turn clockwise, looking straight at that face.
  • ' (prime): a quarter anticlockwise. 2: half a turn.

What you can do

  • Done ✓ once you have made the turn on your cube. The → key or Enter work too.
  • If the step is an algorithm of several turns, you go one turn at a time: at the top you will see “turn 2 of 8”, the 3D cube shows just that turn and the button says “next turn” until the last one. That way you go at your own pace and can learn it.
  • ‹ Back goes back one turn (← key); from the first one, it goes back to the last turn of the previous step. Undo the turn on your cube too.
  • Click a particular turn of the sequence to go to it, and ↻ to see it again.
info.sticker.title: Sticker graph
info.sticker.html:
Here the cube is drawn as a graph: each of the 54 stickers is a vertex, and the grey lines are the paths the stickers move along when you turn a face.

How to read it

  • The 9 points that form a group are one face. The three faces you see head-on on your cube sit in the middle, and the three hidden ones are spread round the edge.
  • Each turn moves 12 stickers round an outer ring and rotates the 8 of the face itself. In mathematics, those rings are the cycles of a permutation.
  • During the animation the turn's ring lights up and you will see the points slide along it three places (six for a half turn, and the other way for a prime turn).

What it is for

To see at a glance how much one turn scrambles: it moves 20 stickers at once, which is why solving the cube by intuition is so hard. When the cube is solved, every group will have its nine points in the same colour.

On a computer, hovering over a point tells you which sticker it is, for example U6.
info.neighbors.title: Neighbours of your vertex
info.neighbors.html:
The blue point in the middle is you: the current position of your cube. Each line is a possible move, and it leads to a neighbouring vertex.

The numbers

  • In the learning mode it is the exact distance to this stage's goal, worked out beforehand with BFS. The number in the middle is yours.
  • In the fast mode it is a lower bound: a number that is never greater than the real distance. It is used to rule out paths without exploring them.

The colours

  • Green: that move takes you closer to the goal.
  • Grey: it leaves you just as far. Red: it takes you further.
  • Thick blue: the edge we have chosen.
  • Dashed line (only in phase 2 of the fast mode): that move would take you out of the subgroup you are already in, so it is not used.

A surprising detail

In the fast mode, sometimes the chosen edge is not the one that lowers the number the most. That is normal: there the number is only an estimate from below, and the search has already explored the whole path, so it knows something the estimate cannot see.
info.levels.title: Layers of the graph
info.levels.html:
It groups every vertex of this stage's graph by its distance to the goal. Bar 0 is the goal, bar 1 the positions solved with one move, and so on.

How to read it

  • The height is how many vertices there are at that distance, on a logarithmic scale: each mark on the left multiplies by ten.
  • The blue bar marked “you” is where you are now. With each step you move one bar to the left.
  • On a computer, hovering over a bar tells you the exact number.

The interesting part

Almost every vertex piles up in the tallest bars, and very few are close to the goal. That is why scrambling is easy and solving is hard: if you turn at random, you almost certainly end up far away. In the fast mode, this chart is the pattern database: a reduced graph that was explored whole with BFS so that distances in the big one, far too huge to explore, can be estimated.
info.path.title: Your path
info.path.html:
It is the whole route from your scrambled cube to the solved one, step by step from left to right. The blue point is where you are.

How to read it

  • The height is what is left. When it reaches the bottom, you are done.
  • The blue part is what you have covered, the grey part what is left.
  • The dotted vertical lines separate the stages. In the learning mode you will see the height jump up when a new stage begins: you are not doing worse, a different graph starts and the count starts again.
  • In the fast mode, the dashed line is the lower bound, always below what is really left.
info.tutor.title: The tutor
info.tutor.html:
Two ways of asking.

The quick questions

The buttons below (what this turn means, why, how much is left, replay and I'm lost) do not go through any model: they are answered from the data of the path worked out, so they are always right and work even when the model is down.

Free question

What you type goes to a language model that is given the context of the step you are on (the stage, the move, the distances and the neighbours). Before its answer is shown, it is checked that it does not tell you to make a turn that is not part of this step or its neighbours; if it does, you see the exact explanation of the step instead.

The coloured dot

  • Green: the model is answering. Next to it you will see which one and how long it took to answer the check.
  • Red: it is not available, and the text says why. Click the dot to check again.
  • Grey: no model is configured in this deployment.

What to ask it

  • “Why this turn and not another?”
  • “What is the subgroup H?”
  • “I can't find the piece you mean, how do I recognise it?”

Careful: the tutor can be wrong. The moves the application gives you are calculated and checked; the tutor's explanations are not. If something does not add up, trust the step card.
info.capture.title: How your cube is read
info.capture.html:
With the camera, the cube is read one face at a time: six steps, each with one face straight on. It is much more reliable than trying to read three faces at once from a corner, which is how it began and did not work with real cubes.

How each step works

  • Show the face straight on, filling a good part of the picture. The application finds the 9 stickers, marks them with their colour and moves on by itself to the next face.
  • A sticker is accepted when it reads the same several times, so a blurred frame does not count.
  • If you are too quick and have not turned the cube yet, it tells you: it does not store the same face twice.
  • If a sticker will not read (a reflection on it), move the cube a little. After a few seconds it reads it anyway from where the grid says it is.

The order of the faces

  • First the four sides, turning the same way and keeping the same face on top. Then the top and the bottom, tilting the cube.
  • There is some slack: if a face comes out turned, or you turned the cube the other way, or showed the bottom where it asked for the top, it works it out at the end and tells you what it assumed.
  • What it cannot do is guess any order at all, and it is worth knowing why: six loose faces do not say how they were joined. With the faces shuffled there are 24 different legal cubes made of your very stickers and only one is yours; picking one would be a 1 in 24 gamble that sends you turning faces for nothing. What does say it is the order you show them in, and that is why the order is kept.
  • What does matter is not repeating a face, and it takes care of that itself: if you show it one it already has, it tells you and does not record it again. To recognise it, it does not compare the colours as they are (under another light the same white changes more than white and yellow differ), but the hue of each sticker, which does not change when the light goes up or down, and it tries the four turns of the face in case you show it turned. It looks at the nine on average, not at the one that fits worst: if a reflection spoils one sticker, the other eight decide. If it still gets it wrong, there is the “No, it's another face: use it” button.
  • And at the end there is one last check: six faces must be six different faces. It compares the fifteen pairs and, if one stands out for being alike, it asks for that face again instead of sending you on to the next screen with an impossible cube.

If a face just will not work

Adjust by hand freezes the picture and you place the 4 corners of the face; the circles show you the colour each sticker reads. After 18 seconds it takes you there by itself.

Uploading photos instead of using the camera, two photos are still asked for, each with a corner pointing at the camera, with the same manual adjustment if needed.
info.review.title: Checking the colours
info.review.html:
The cube unfolded, as if you opened it out into a cross. At the top the top face, in the middle the front one, and the one at the far right is the back.

How to correct

  • Pick a colour in the palette and click the sticker that is wrong.
  • The number on each colour of the palette counts how many times it appears: there must be nine of each. If it shows in red, one is missing or there is one too many.
  • The centres cannot move on a real cube: they are what define the colour of each face.

How the colours are read (and why it almost never comes out impossible)

Each sticker is not classified on its own. A cube is not 54 loose colours: it is eight corners and twelve edges, and we know exactly which ones exist, because the centres give the six colours. Each corner is a combination of {top,bottom} × {right,left} × {front,back}, and each piece is on the cube exactly once.

So the question is not “what colour is this sticker?” but “which piece is in this corner?”, answered for all eight at once with a minimum-cost assignment. A red read as orange no longer breaks anything: the piece it would make is already taken, and the next cheapest reading wins. In tests, this went from 71% to 100% of valid cubes.

Also, each face is scanned under its own light (the camera adjusts the exposure as the cube turns). That is estimated and corrected, because a red under one light can land closer to the orange of another.

If it says the cube is impossible

We check that it is a cube that can be reached by turning faces (no repeated pieces, correct orientations and parity). If the message appears, it is almost always a misread colour, not a broken cube. The message tells you which piece to look at. The orientation of the second photo can also be wrong: that is what the button that tries another one is for.

Stickers with a dashed border are the ones the structure of the cube had to correct: the camera said something else. They are usually right, but that is where I would look first.
info.mode.title: Which mode should I choose?
info.mode.html:
Learn, layer by layer

The classic beginner's method, in 7 stages: bottom cross, bottom corners, second layer and the four steps of the last layer. It takes some 100 to 140 turns, but the algorithms repeat and you end up learning them. Each stage is a small graph with exact distances, so you always see how much is really left.

Fast, Kociemba in two phases

About 20 or 22 turns, close to the least possible (no cube needs more than 20). It does not teach you to solve, because the moves do not follow a pattern you can remember, but it is the shortest path and shows very well how a search with lower bounds works.

The colour of the first layer

Only in the learning mode: choose which face you start from. White is the usual one. The application will tell you how to hold the cube before you start.
info.button_title: What this is and how to use it
tech.v.animation: a 90° turn about the face's axis; at the end the cubies go back to their places and the state is repainted
tech.v.state: a string of 54 letters (faces U R F D L B); each turn is a permutation of those 54 positions
tech.v.cycles: a ring of 12 stickers (moves on 3) and a cycle of 8 on the face itself (moves on 2)
tech.v.projection: Lambert azimuthal equal-area, centred on the corner pointing at the camera
tech.v.groups: the Schreier graph of the cube group's action on the 54 stickers
tech.v.learn_numbers: exact distance to the goal, worked out beforehand with BFS from the goal following the edges backwards
tech.v.fast_numbers: admissible lower bound: the larger of two pattern databases
tech.v.bfs_exact: full BFS from the goal; each vertex's distance is exact
tech.v.db_bfs: full BFS in the reduced graph, stored as a table
tech.v.db_use: a lower bound that never exceeds the real distance, to prune the IDA* search
tech.v.height: distance to the goal of the current stage; it starts again at each new stage
tech.v.descent: descent along the distance function: each edge lowers it by exactly 1
tech.v.dashed: lower bound; the solid one is the turns really left
tech.v.tutor_check: GET /v1/models with a 6 s limit, cached for 30 s on the server
tech.v.tutor_context: mode, stage, goal, chosen move, distances and the neighbours with their distance
tech.v.tutor_quick: answered in the browser from the plan's data, with no model and no network
tech.v.tutor_answer_check: turns in notation (R, U', F2…) are looked for in the answer and compared with those of the step and its neighbours; an invented one replaces the answer with the plan's explanation
tech.v.tutor_warning: the model can be wrong in its explanations; the moves do not come from it but from the solver
tech.v.detection: the holes of the black frame (and, as an alternative, the patches of colour) are segmented at three scales
tech.v.grid: the directions of the grid come from the patches themselves: a histogram of angles between neighbours, and each patch is projected to its row and column
tech.v.resolution: 480 px wide for analysis; 6 segmentations tried per frame
tech.v.reading: each sticker is fixed when 3 readings agree; if one resists for 7 s, it is read from where the grid says it is
tech.v.repeats: mean distance over the 9 stickers in Lab, with hue counting in full and lightness and chroma less (light changes those, not the hue); under the 4 turns and dropping the worst. Decided against the second most similar face: a repeat is under 0.62 times the distance of the next one
tech.v.colours: the same hue-based distance: in photos of the real cube, a red washed out by the window came out closer to an orange than to another red with the plain Lab distance, and not with this one
tech.v.fingers: a sticker that is not seen (nearly always a finger over it) and is read off the grid counts a quarter: in real photos, 11 of 13 skin samples came out closest to red
tech.v.last_check: at the end the 15 pairs of faces are compared: a repeat is not only close to its twin, it is twice as close as any other pair, and that does not depend on the cube's colours or the light
tech.v.review_reading: not sticker by sticker but piece by piece: 8 corners and 12 edges assigned at minimum cost (Hungarian algorithm), each piece used exactly once
tech.v.light: each face is scanned with its own exposure, so a gain per face is estimated in turn with the classification (6 rounds) until they are all under the same light
tech.v.checks: 9 stickers per colour, different centres, no repeated pieces
tech.v.orientations: sum of corner twists ≡ 0 (mod 3) and of edge flips ≡ 0 (mod 2)
tech.v.parity: the corner permutation and the edge permutation must have the same parity
tech.v.photo2: the 3 possible orientations are tried and the one giving a possible cube is chosen
tech.v.holding: 4 ways of holding it × 4 turns per face (4,096 combinations), pruned by corners and edges; if two fit, you are warned
tech.v.repair: the three laws (corner twists a multiple of 3, edge flips a multiple of 2, equal parities) say which one fails, and only the changes that could mend it are tried, cheapest first
tech.v.mode_learn: 7 stages; graphs of 24 to 190,080 vertices; BFS from the goal; about 100-140 turns
tech.v.mode_fast: IDA* in G/H ({g} vertices) and then inside H ({h}); 20-22 turns
tech.v.bounds: pattern databases computed with BFS and stored in the container image
